skill.name: A problem that gets worse
skill.why: Stories get exciting when things go wrong, then go even more wrong.
skill.how: Give your character a problem. Each fix they try makes it worse.

steps.say: I wrote a whole story. It is very short. Can you see why?
steps.ask: Why is my story over so fast?

options.reason: The story never says how big the dog is. Look at what Mum does.

options.text: The problem gets fixed straight away.

options.reason: Lunch can be funny! Look at what happens right after the problem.

steps.win: Yes! One line of trouble, one line of fix. The problem in a story is also called the complication.

steps.say: So I tried again. This time, my fix goes wrong.

show.nudge: That's where the trouble starts. Read on. What goes wrong next?
That's my fix. What happened because of it?

show.text: He ran into the neighbour's pool.

steps.ask: Tap the part where things get worse.
steps.win: Yes! My fix made it worse. Now there is a wet dog and an angry neighbour.

steps.say: Now the dog is in the pool. Make it worse again!

show.text: He ran into the neighbour's pool.

steps.ask: Which line makes it worse again?

options.text: The dog climbed out of the pool, and everything was fine again.
options.reason: That fixes it. Is anyone in more trouble now?

options.text: My favourite colour is green, and I like blue as well.
options.reason: That's a random fact. It has nothing to do with the dog or the pool.

options.text: I jumped in to get him, and the neighbour's alarm went off.

steps.win: Yes! Each step makes the trouble bigger. Lunch, then the pool, then the alarm.

steps.say: Zed wants a happy surprise next. Nice, right? Let's check what it does to the story.

show.text: Then a kind man gave me his lunch.

steps.ask: What does Zed's line do to the story?

options.text: It ends the trouble too soon.

options.reason: Is anyone in more trouble now? Or is lunch sorted?
A free lunch isn't a problem! It solves one.

steps.win: Right. Lucky help ends the story too early. Save the real fix for the very end.

steps.say: Here is the trick from my slime story. Watch what my own fix does.

show.text: The slime slid into the air vent.
show.nudge: That's the trouble. Which part is me trying to fix it?

show.text: I turned on the fan to blow it out.
The fan sprayed slime all over the ship.
show.nudge: That's what happened next. What did I do that caused it?

steps.ask: Tap the part where I try to fix it.
steps.win: Yes! The fan was my fix, and it caused the next problem. That is how trouble grows.

steps.say: Mo spilt glue on his homework. He tried to dry it with a hair dryer.

show.text: Mo dried the glue with a hair dryer.

steps.ask: Which line makes it worse, because of Mo's fix?

options.text: Then a spaceship landed on the school.
options.reason: That's big trouble, but Mo's fix didn't cause it. It came from nowhere.

options.text: The hair dryer blew his pages all over the street.
The glue dried, and the homework was fine.
options.reason: That fixes it too soon. Is Mo in more trouble?

steps.win: Yes! His own fix caused it. In your story, start each step: 'That made it worse, because…'

terms.means: The trouble at the start. Also called the complication.
What the character tries, to solve the problem.
What goes wrong because of the fix. The trouble gets bigger.
Lucky help that ends the trouble too soon.

examples.text: He ran into the neighbour's pool.
It sprayed slime all over the ship.

card.test: After each fix, ask: is my character in more trouble now? Save the real fix for the end.

weDo.frame: Gus is helping Mo write up his worst day in the galley.
weDo.text: Mo's cake was stuck in the oven. He pulled the handle hard.
weDo.prompt: Which next sentence makes the problem worse?
weDo.hint: Which one leaves Mo in more trouble?
weDo.success: Now Mo can't open the oven, and the cake is burning. The problem just got bigger.

options.text: The handle snapped off, and smoke began to pour out.
The door opened easily, and the cake was perfect.
options.reason: That fixes the problem straight away, so the tension disappears.
It's a random fact. It doesn't push the problem forward at all.

weDo.frame: Tully's footy is stuck on the school roof. Gus is planning what happens next.
weDo.prompt: Put each event in the right bin.
weDo.hint: Does Tully end up in more trouble, or out of it?
weDo.success: Bending pipes, flying shoes and a stuck Tully make the trouble bigger. Easy rescues end the story too early.

items.text: She climbs the drainpipe, and it starts to bend.
items.reason: A bending pipe puts Tully in danger, so things get worse.

items.text: A teacher hands her a spare footy.
items.reason: A spare footy solves it instantly, and the story's over.

items.text: Her shoe falls off and lands in the principal's coffee.
items.reason: Now there's a second problem, and it belongs to the principal!

items.text: The wind blows the footy back down to her.
items.reason: Lucky wind fixes everything, so there's no tension left.

items.text: Now Tully is stuck on the roof too.
items.reason: The rescuer needs rescuing. That's much worse!

creature.name: Brinkle
creature.blurb: A speck of sea sparkle that glows brighter every time the water is stirred. One splash, then two, and soon the whole bay is blazing.

workshop.mentor: It started with one sneeze. Gus had been holding a jar of Creature slime, and the sneeze sent the lid spinning across the lab. The slime didn't stay in the jar. It slid down the bench, across the floor and straight into the air vent. 'Not a problem,' said Gus, and turned on the fan to blow it back out. That was a problem. The fan sprayed slime through every vent on the ship. It dripped into Zed's game console. It glued Mo's frying pan to the ceiling. It landed in Tully's hair, which turned bright green. And then, from somewhere deep in the walls, the slime began to sing.
workshop.ask: Write a story where each fix makes things worse. Ideas: a sneeze in Gus's lab, a footy on the roof, a snake loose in class, one tiny lie.
checklist: I gave my character a problem early on.
I made the first fix go wrong.
I made things worse at least twice.
I saved the solution for the end.
